text: Defender for Office 365 is the Defender XDR workload that protects email and collaboration tools — Exchange Online, SharePoint, OneDrive, and Teams. It exists because email remains the most common way an attacker gets an initial foothold: a convincing message is cheaper to send than an exploit is to build, and it only has to work once.

A malicious link doesn't have to be malicious the moment it arrives. An attacker can send a link to a page that's clean at delivery, then weaponize it later once the email has already passed every filter. Safe Links defends against exactly that, rewriting URLs in email, documents, and Teams messages and re-checking the destination at the moment someone actually clicks it, not just once on arrival.

Safe Attachments targets the other classic vector: a malicious file riding along with a normal-looking email. Instead of only scanning statically for a known signature, it opens the attachment in an isolated sandbox and watches what it actually does, a technique called detonation, before the message is ever delivered to the inbox.

Not every email attack needs a link or a file at all. Business Email Compromise is pure social engineering — a message impersonating an executive or vendor, asking someone in finance to redirect a wire transfer, with no malware for Safe Attachments and no link for Safe Links to check.

That's what anti-phishing policies are for. Using impersonation detection and mailbox intelligence — learning a mailbox's normal senders and patterns — Defender for Office 365 can flag a message that claims to be from the CFO but doesn't match how the CFO's real mail actually behaves, even with nothing technical to scan.

Go back to the attack chain from Lesson 17: it started with a phishing email, and that's not a coincidence. Safe Links, Safe Attachments, and anti-phishing policies each defend a different shape of email attack, and an attacker only needs one of them to fail once to get the foothold the rest of the chain builds on.
